case_study_insert.main_stem: Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic (RPS) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, specialising in physiotherapy and sports rehabilitation, employing a workforce of 31. Founded in 2015 by Dr Natalie Rowan, RPS uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership from its Guildford clinic. RPS plans to invest $540,000 in a second clinic in Woking with a hydrotherapy pool and water-recycling technology, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $342,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.00 a unit and a selling price of $60.00, and currently produces 42,000 units a year (treatment sessions). RPS faces two problems: a skills gap in qualified sports physiotherapists and rising patient complaints about waiting times.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Clinic Operations Report — Q3 2025: The Guildford clinic delivered 10,500 treatment sessions last quarter at a rework error rate of 1.1%, down from 2.4% a year ago. Patient complaints fell from 25 to 14 per month. A survey of 620 patients found 61% would use the new Woking clinic and 47% would pay up to $20 more per session for early-morning appointments. Average waiting time is 12 days. On-the-job training on the new hydrotherapy equipment is incomplete for 11 of 31 staff; off-the-job training courses at the hospital college cost $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.90 to $13.67 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across private healthcare. (3) Medical equipment and consumable costs have risen 9.2% year-on-year, healthcare inflation is running at 6.7%, and consumer spending on private physiotherapy grew 4.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: RPS plans to finance part of its Woking expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for RPS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $240,000 of retained profit instead of borrowing more costs RPS nothing in interest or repayment charges, protecting cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $342,000 a year and a $300,000 five-year bank loan. Every dollar not paid to a lender can absorb the 9.2% rise in medical equipment and consumable costs, helping RPS hold its $60.00 session price and protect the $38.00 contribution per session without squeezing patients or referring clinicians.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $240,000 is available without putting the new $540,000 Woking clinic or its hydrotherapy pool at risk of repossession if demand disappoints. It also preserves Dr Natalie Rowan's ownership and control, since no external lender can impose conditions on how Woking is staffed, marketed or equipped. At a time when the base interest rate has risen from 4.0% to 4.75%, keeping borrowings low also shields RPS's variable-rate loan from further cost increases and keeps the 12-day waiting list affordable to run down.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: RPS is launching its second clinic in Woking with a hydrotherapy pool. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should RPS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national television campaign would put the Rowan Physio & Sports Clinic brand in front of millions of viewers quickly and could build awareness of the hydrotherapy offer. However, RPS is a 31-employee clinic funding a $540,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most viewers live far outside the Guildford–Woking catchment or have no need for private physiotherapy, so most spend would be wasted. Television also suits mass consumer brands rather than appointment-led healthcare, where local trust and clinician reputation drive bookings.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper, reaches Guildford and Woking commuters repeatedly, and suits appointment-led messages such as early-morning sessions and waiting-time reductions. Its limitation is reach beyond the catchment — patients travel from across Surrey and Hampshire for specialist sports rehabilitation, so a purely local station cannot fill the Woking hydrotherapy pool or build county-wide referral relationships with clubs and gyms.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with local sports clubs, fitness creators and post-injury recovery bloggers targets exactly the 61% of surveyed patients who would use the Woking clinic and the 47% willing to pay up to $20 more per session for early-morning appointments. Content can show real recoveries, cost per reached patient is low, engagement is measurable through booking codes, and the water-recycling and sustainability story of the hydrotherapy pool gives influencers distinctive material. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but the audience match is far better.

Recommendation: RPS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment identified in its research (61% Woking interest, 47% early-morning premium), costs far less than television for a 31-person clinic, scales across the county where local radio cannot, and showcases the hydrotherapy pool effectively. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is too narrow for county-wide sports-referral growth, though short Woking drive-time bursts could support the launch. Influencers alone lack broadcast reach, so RPS should pair them with club partnerships and GP referral letters.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RPS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RPS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: RPS faces a skills gap in qualified sports physiotherapists and rising complaints about waiting times. Explain two benefits for RPS of its democratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives RPS's 31 staff a genuine voice in how rota planning, triage protocols and the new hydrotherapy pool are organised, satisfying esteem and belonging needs (Maslow) and raising job satisfaction. Physiotherapists who help design session templates and waiting-list priorities are more likely to stay in post, directly attacking the skills gap in qualified sports staff and helping stabilise the 12-day average waiting time that is driving complaints.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions generates practical suggestions from the people who handle patients daily, improving the 1.1% rework error rate further and pushing complaints (down from 25 to 14 per month) lower still. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers turnover in scarce clinical roles, saving the $950 per employee retraining cost at the hospital college and protecting output of 42,000 treatment sessions a year while the Woking clinic and pool bed in and the 11 under-trained staff complete their hydrotherapy training.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RPS's skills gap, waiting times, rework rate and output.

questions.question_text: RPS must train 11 clinic staff on the new hydrotherapy equipment. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the hospital college. Which should RPS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training alongside experienced physios in the Guildford clinic is directly relevant to RPS's own hydrotherapy pool, safety checks and patient-handling routines, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 11 staff treating patients, protecting delivery of 10,500 sessions last quarter and the fall in rework errors from 2.4% to 1.1%. Drawbacks are that trainers are serving clinicians whose own caseloads suffer, bad habits on the pool equipment can pass between colleagues, and formal certification is limited — an issue if the hydrotherapy pool's insurer or regulators require documented competence before Woking opens.

Off-the-job training: The hospital college course at $950 per employee gives structured, current hydrotherapy content and a recognised certificate for all 11 staff, costing $10,450 in total — affordable against a $540,000 expansion. It removes clinicians from the treatment floor, however, reducing short-term capacity and risking a longer 12-day waiting time, and the generic college content may not match RPS's exact pool settings, jet positions and safety interlocks, so follow-up on-site coaching would still be needed.

Decision: RPS should choose on-the-job training for the initial Woking rollout, supported by off-the-job college places for two senior physios who can then cascade safe pool operation to the rest of the team. On-the-job training is cheaper, pool-specific and avoids pulling a third of the clinical workforce off the floor while waiting times are a complaint driver. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 11 staff and spending $10,450 up front would deepen the 12-day waiting-time problem and delay the Woking launch; college certification can be layered on once the pool is operational and demand stabilises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to RPS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of RPS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of RPS with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, certification and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RPS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $342,000 ÷ ($60.00 − $22.00) = $342,000 ÷ $38.00 = 9,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 9,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $60.00 − $22.00 = $38.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $38.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RPS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. RPS's managers can compare the 9,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 42,000 treatment sessions to confirm the clinic is safely profitable, with a margin of safety of 33,000 sessions, informing how fast the Woking clinic can ramp up without over-stretching cash.
2. Contribution per unit of $38.00 lets managers model the effect of the early-morning premium, for example charging $20 more for dawn slots would lift contribution toward $58.00 on those sessions, letting managers judge whether the 47% of patients willing to pay more would fill enough slots to cover the $342,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution per unit helps managers set session-volume targets used to justify the $300,000 bank loan and the $240,000 retained-profit contribution, checking the Woking pool can service both before the launch is announced to patients.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($342,000 ÷ 42,000 units + $22.00 = $30.14 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, identify waste in consumables amid the 9.2% input-cost inflation, and compare cost per session between Guildford and Woking once the new clinic opens.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 9,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $38.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 33,000 sessions vs 42,000-session output; early-morning premium modelling vs $342,000 fixed costs; loan feasibility for the $540,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $30.14 across the two clinics.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RPS's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has RPS's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 10.0%
ROCE 2025 = 14.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $880,000 on revenue $2,200,000 (cost of sales $1,320,000); 2025 gross profit $1,134,000 on revenue $2,520,000 (cost of sales $1,386,000). 2024 operating profit $330,000; 2025 operating profit $504,000. 2024 capital employed $3,300,000; 2025 capital employed $3,600,000. Interest payable rose from $20,000 to $28,000, reflecting the five-year bank loan funding the Woking clinic.

Evaluation: Performance improved strongly. Gross profit grew $254,000 (28.9%) as revenue rose $320,000 and the cost of sales share of revenue fell from 60.0% to 55.0%, helped by the rework error rate falling from 2.4% to 1.1% and complaints from 25 to 14 a month. Operating profit grew 52.7% ($330,000 to $504,000), well ahead of revenue growth of 14.5%, so overheads were absorbed more efficiently from the single Guildford site. Capital employed rose $300,000 on the Woking pool with water-recycling technology, yet the return on that capital still strengthened from 10.0% to 14.0%. However, interest payable is rising with the loan and the base-rate move from 4.0% to 4.75%, the 9.2% medical equipment inflation could pressure future cost of sales, and Woking's ramp-up carries the risk that pool sessions fill more slowly than the 61% patient interest suggests.

Conclusion: Yes, RPS's financial performance has improved. Revenue, gross profit and operating profit all grew, cost control genuinely improved, and the return on capital employed climbed from 10.0% to 14.0% while still funding expansion. The judgement is not risk-free — borrowing is costlier and equipment inflation is outpacing price rises — so RPS should monitor Woking's fill rate weekly, control consumable spend and close the skills gap urgently, but the overall verdict is a clearly improved performance.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, overheads and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether RPS's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RPS of installing water-recycling technology for its hydrotherapy pool.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Water-recycling cuts the pool's water and heating bills, directly lowering the $342,000 fixed-cost base and freeing cash to fund the $540,000 Woking expansion rather than diverting scarce funds to utility suppliers. It also strengthens RPS's environmental image — differentiating the clinic from competitors without a pool, appealing to the 61% of surveyed patients willing to use Woking, and supporting staff pride in working for a sustainable healthcare provider amid a 31-person workforce competing for scarce physiotherapists.

Disadvantage: The technology adds an upfront cost on top of an already stretched $540,000 project funded partly by a $300,000 bank loan, increasing immediate cash strain and the amount RPS must repay. Filtration and recycling systems also need specialist servicing and monitoring; any failure in water quality halts hydrotherapy sessions, breaks the 12-day waiting-time promise, and raises hygiene and liability risks that could undermine patient trust in the new Woking clinic before it gains momentum.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RPS's costs, demand data and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 9.2% rise in input costs will affect RPS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If RPS's $300,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $2,250 a year to financing costs — real but modest next to $342,000 of fixed costs. Higher rates also make further borrowing for a third clinic more expensive, may temper consumer appetite for elective private physiotherapy, and could slow the 4.2% growth in private physio spending. RPS can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate or accelerating retained-profit repayments.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.67 per hour): RPS employs 31 staff; physiotherapists earn well above minimum wage, but reception, cleaning and support roles are affected. If roughly 10 of the 31 staff sit near the minimum wage on 40-hour weeks, the 6.0% rise adds roughly $1,610 per affected worker a year — around $16,000 a year — on top of the skills gap in sports physios and the $950-per-head retraining bill at the hospital college. The impact is material but concentrated in support roles.

Input cost inflation (9.2% medical equipment and consumables): RPS's variable cost of $22.00 a unit is dominated by sterile consumables, tapes, resistive bands and single-use hydrotherapy items. A 9.2% rise on the consumable share (say 65% of variable cost, $14.30) adds roughly $1.32 per session; at 42,000 sessions a year that is about $55,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $38.00 toward $36.68 and eroding roughly 3.5% of margin. With 4.2% growth in private physio spending, RPS can pass on part of this through the $20 early-morning premium (the 47% willing to pay more), but full pass-through would test patient loyalty against NHS alternatives.

Conclusion: The 9.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 42,000 sessions, totalling roughly $55,000 a year and steadily eroding the $38.00 contribution margin that justifies the $540,000 Woking expansion. The minimum wage rise is the second risk, roughly $16,000 a year concentrated in support roles, while the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms (about $2,250 a year) and can be managed by fixing the loan rate. RPS should still act on all three — renegotiate consumable contracts, redesign support rosters and review the loan structure — or the improved cost-of-sales performance shown in Appendix 2 will unwind by 2026.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to RPS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RPS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of RPS with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
